phase2.title: Look for the watermark
phase2.explanation: Before focusing on any other detail in the image, check the corners: many AI generators add a discreet watermark. Gemini, for example, usually places its watermark in the bottom-right corner. Tools like SynthID also embed marks that are invisible to the naked eye but detectable with the right tools.

phase2.title: From counting fingers to reading tricky hands
phase2.explanation: Counting fingers used to be enough, but current models already generate correct hands in normal poses. Now look at complex interactions instead: interlaced fingers, hands holding a small object, or hands partially covered by hair or clothing. Look at the girl's hands holding the sandwich: it seems to float instead of actually being gripped, a sign that the AI didn't quite understand the contact between the hand and the object.

phase2.title: Background text no longer gives it away
phase2.explanation: Perfect skin or symmetrical eye highlights no longer give away an AI image. What still fails is background text: signs, posters, or book spines that look normal at first glance, but up close the letters are malformed or make no sense at all.

phase2.title: Patterns that break
phase2.explanation: Bricks, tiles, fabrics, or fences should repeat with mathematical regularity. In AI-generated images, the pattern often loses that regularity or even shows a visible seam halfway through the image, where the design changes abruptly.

phase2.title: Shadows and reflections that don't add up
phase2.explanation: Check whether the shadow points toward the light source visible in the image, and whether reflections in glass, water, or metal show the same scene a real reflection would. Inconsistent light physics remains one of the most reliable tells.

phase2.title: Repeated background elements
phase2.explanation: In scenes with crowds or detailed backgrounds, look for faces or people that repeat almost identically, or details duplicated in an unnatural way. AI models tend to clone background elements instead of generating unique variations for each one.

phase2.title: That too-perfect color
phase2.explanation: Many AI models have a recognizable default style: more saturated colors than normal, high contrast, and an almost plasticky finish, as if everything were over-lit. If a photo looks "too pretty" or has a palette that's too uniform to be real, that's as valid a clue as any specific detail.

phase2.title: Want to learn more?
phase2.explanation: None of this is perfect or foolproof: models keep improving and these signals may stop working at any moment. In the end, you have to use your common sense and notice whether what you see feels coherent, or whether something just doesn't add up. If you want to dig deeper, here are some resources to stay up to date on the latest signals for spotting AI-generated images: How to Spot an AI-Generated Image in 2026 (https://www.opticflux.com/how-to-spot-an-ai-generated-image-in-2026-the-tells-that-still-work/79504/), How to Spot AI-Generated Images in 2026: Artifacts, C2PA & SynthID (https://www.eyesift.com/blog/how-to-spot-ai-images-2026/), 9 Common AI Image Artifacts: Spot & Fix (https://zsky.ai/blog/ai-image-artifacts-guide), and How to Tell if an Image Is AI-Generated in 2026 (https://endertech.com/blog/6-ways-to-identify-ai-generated-images-with-examples).
